chunks.text: Zamia pygmaea holds the distinction of being the smallest cycad known, with some wild individuals reaching only about 25 centimetres in total height. Unlike most cycads, which build an obvious trunk above ground, this species keeps almost all of its short, thickened stem buried below the soil surface, sending up only a modest crown of one to four stiff, leathery compound leaves in harsh wild conditions — cultivated plants, given better soil and water, can produce up to twenty leaves and noticeably more vigorous growth, each leaf bearing between five and fifteen pairs of small oval leaflets. It is endemic to western Cuba and the adjacent Isla de la Juventud, where it grows in some of the driest, most exposed habitats available to any Zamia species: open serpentine and limestone outcrops, sun-baked pine savanna, and coastal sand, from sea level up to about 200 metres. The IUCN rates it Critically Endangered, estimating fewer than 250 mature plants left in the wild, threatened by illegal collection, habitat loss to agriculture and ranching, and general deforestation; it survives today partly within two protected reserves on Cuban territory. Locally the plant and its relatives are known by names like guayiga or guayra, Spanish terms of likely Tainó origin first recorded around 1550 by the chronicler Bartolomé de las Casas; some of these old names, such as 'yuquilla de ratón', literally reference the plant's toxicity, and the same root may underlie the Spanish verb guayar, 'to grate', from the historical practice of grating toxic Zamia stems to prepare a starch bread after careful detoxification.

chunks.source: Botanical Survey of India — Chromosome Database (Gymnosperms): Zamia pygmaea datasheet
chunks.text: This Indian government botanical reference situates Zamia pygmaea within its chromosome and distribution database of gymnosperms, recording it as a species endemic to western Cuba and the Isla de la Juventud — consistent with international sources — and noting that it is maintained under cultivation in India at the Botanical Garden of the National Botanical Research Institute (NBRI) in Lucknow, Uttar Pradesh, presumably as part of a living reference and conservation collection rather than for any commercial or amenity purpose. Its inclusion in a national chromosome database also implies that karyotype data for the species has been recorded or is being tracked by Indian botanical researchers, reflecting the broader scientific interest cycads attract as living representatives of an ancient plant lineage that predates flowering plants. That such a narrowly distributed, critically endangered Caribbean dwarf cycad is deliberately grown in an Indian national botanical garden illustrates how ex-situ cultivation in botanical institutions around the world has become an important supplementary safeguard for cycad species whose wild populations are small and vulnerable to further decline.
